replacement_html:
4.2.7b The dome's eclipse coverage numbers, checked against the actual eclipse

The dome has published three different "coverage" tables for the same stations and the same eclipse. Its oldest table, labelled LOCKED and now archived, matched the real eclipse to within 7 percentage points. The current tables put the northern stations 31 to 46 points too low. The dome's formula multiplies by coverage, so its predicted signals at those stations drop by up to half. The home page says the signal will appear "at 7 magnetic observatories with >80% eclipse coverage"; that is true of the real eclipse, but by the dome's own table only three of the seven are above 80%.

Every per-station magnetic prediction the dome makes for 12 August 2026 has the form baseline × coverage × FSF. Section 4.2.7a showed that the dome's own geometry gives a shadow that misses every one of its stations. This section asks a simpler question: whatever the source of the coverage numbers, are they right?

How we checked

"Coverage" here means obscuration: the fraction of the Sun's disc area hidden by the Moon at the moment of greatest eclipse at the station. We computed it for each station from the JPL DE421 ephemeris (skyfield), once a minute from 15:00 to 21:00 UT. We also give the magnitude, the fraction of the Sun's diameter covered, which runs a little higher. The Hartland result, 94.4%, matches the figure in 4.2.7. Script, inputs and output hashes are in the analysis record.

Sources: predictions page station tables (nine-station version registered in our frozen prediction file, claim B2-M-001); home page station table (re-checked 2026-10-04); AI context archive page, table "Eclipse PRED-001 through PRED-008 (LOCKED, Aug 12 2026)". The obscuration is the geometric maximum. At Ebro, Niemegk and Buděkov the Sun is less than 5° above the horizon at that moment.

What the dome gets right

The numbers are not random. On the seven mainland stations of the predictions-page table the order is exactly right: rank the stations by the dome's coverage and by the real eclipse and you get the same list. The two Spanish stations and Coimbra are within 9 points. The oldest table, PRED-001 to PRED-005, is within 7 points at all five stations it covers (4 points on average). That is the accuracy you get by reading an eclipse calculator built on the standard ephemeris. It is not what the dome's own geometry gives (4.2.7a). The stations and their order came from the globe.

What went wrong

The dome made the change openly. The task list on its AI context page reads: "Fix PRED-001-008 eclipse predictions — V9 ESK/LER coverage wrong (0.98/0.92 should be 0.55/0.42)", followed by "Push V12 eclipse predictions (E001-E009) as replacement". Since 2026-04-17 that page is labelled an archive, and the dome names the predictions page as the source of truth. So the registered values are the new ones. But the old values were 7 and 4 points from the real eclipse, and the new ones are 36 and 46 points off. The "fix" moved them away from the eclipse. The dome gives no derivation for the new numbers, and neither obscuration nor magnitude reproduces them. Niemegk is in the same position: 0.40 against an actual 85%.

This matters because coverage multiplies straight into the predicted signal. With the dome's own BOU baseline (−10.9 nT) and its own FSF values, the predicted signal at Lerwick is −9.5 nT on the dome's coverage and −20.0 nT on the real one. Eskdalemuir goes from −10.3 to −17.1 nT and Niemegk from −6.7 to −14.2 nT. Ebro barely moves (−10.7 to −11.2 nT). Our evaluation of the 12 August data runs every test with both sets of coverage, so this section does not decide any verdict. One sub-test is unaffected: the dome's E-PRED-B ("Hartland beats Ebro despite lower coverage") holds on either set, 1.18 against 0.98 on the dome's numbers and 1.39 against 1.03 on the real ones.

The home page disagrees with the predictions page

The home page lists seven stations under the sentence "At 7 magnetic observatories with >80% eclipse coverage". By the coverage figures in its own table, three are above 80% (Ebro, San Pablo, Chambon) and Hartland sits at exactly 80%. By the real eclipse, all seven are above 80%; the lowest is Niemegk at 85%. The sentence is true of the actual eclipse and false of the dome's numbers. Three of its seven coverage figures also differ from the predictions page, which the dome itself names as the source of truth (Chambon 85% against 0.70, Niemegk 72% against 0.40, Eskdalemuir 60% against 0.55), and Buděkov is not on the predictions page at all.

The home page's predicted ranges fall in step with coverage, with no sign of the FSF. Hartland gets −13 to −17 nT and Ebro −17 to −21 nT, so Hartland is smaller. That is the reverse of E-PRED-B, which the predictions page marks LOCKED. The home page also gives the globe prediction as "0.0 nT exactly. No mechanism", while the predictions page's Tier-1 block says "or ionospheric Sq disruption — competing mechanism exists". Standard physics does predict an eclipse signal, from the ionospheric currents (4.2.3).

How many predictions for Ebro?

For Ebro, the station the dome's PRED-095 card names first, the current (non-archived) pages give five figures: −10.7 nT (formula with the BOU baseline), −17.8 ± 2 nT (the PRED-095 card), −17 to −21 nT (home page and the predictions page's revised paragraph), −21.7 nT (formula with the −22.24 nT W004 baseline) and −28.9 nT (kill-shot page and the live scoring record). The highest is 2.7 times the lowest; with the archived PRED-001 (−8.4 nT) it is 3.4 times. The step from −10.9 to −18.22 is not itself a contradiction. It is the dome re-measuring its own 2017 Boulder anchor against a quiet-day baseline (audit dated 2026-03-15), which is a reasonable thing to do; 18.22 / 10.9 = 1.672, and the model page says "Multiply all BOU-baseline predictions (E001–E009 BOU column) by 1.67". The same page still says the nine-station predictions "use −10.9 nT as baseline", with the recalculation marked open. The −28.9 nT figure applies the 1.672 factor a second time (6.14, 8.16). The problem is that the uncorrected and the doubled versions stay on current pages next to the corrected one, so a reader cannot tell which number the data are supposed to test (compare the two-baseline hedge in 4.2.3).

kernel_of_truth: The dome's coverage numbers came from somewhere accurate. On the seven mainland stations of the predictions-page table the order is exactly the real eclipse order (Spearman 1.0), the Spanish stations and Coimbra are within 9 pp, and the original V9 LOCKED table was within 7 pp at every station (mean 4.3). The home page's "7 observatories with >80% coverage" is literally true of the real eclipse. The dome was also open about the V9->V12 replacement (task list) and about re-measuring its 2017 anchor (OPEN-009), and it labels the old context page as archive. E-PRED-B survives the coverage correction. The failure is not that the dome invented its stations; it is that the published replacements moved the numbers away from the eclipse and three current pages disagree with each other.

anticipated_objections.objection: "Coverage" in the dome formula is a dome-native quantity, not astronomical obscuration.
anticipated_objections.response: Then it needs a definition and a derivation, and the dome publishes neither. Obscuration and magnitude both fail at ESK/LER/NGK by 36-48 pp. 4.2.7a shows the dome's own shadow geometry gives zero at every station, so no dome-native quantity can be 0.40-0.95 either. And the dome's own home-page sentence ("7 observatories with >80% eclipse coverage") only works with astronomical obscuration.

anticipated_objections.objection: The context page is an archive; citing the V9 table is digging up superseded material.
anticipated_objections.response: Accepted and stated in the prose: the section says the dome names predictions.html as source of truth and that the registered values are the new ones. V9 is cited only to show the direction of the change (accurate -> inaccurate), and the Ebro count is given both with and without the archived figure (2.7x vs 3.4x).

anticipated_objections.objection: Coverage errors are clerical and do not touch the physics.
anticipated_objections.response: They change the dome's own predicted amplitudes by up to a factor 2 (LER -9.5 vs -20.0 nT). The section also says plainly that our results evaluation runs both coverage sets so the verdict does not hinge on this, and that E-PRED-B is unaffected. Clerical or not, the published per-station predictions are what get scored.

anticipated_objections.objection: The home page is a summary for lay readers; its table should not be held to registration standards.
anticipated_objections.response: The home page carries "Timestamp proof: git SHA256 on 2026-03-22" directly under the table (01-home.txt:530) and presents per-station predicted ranges. It is presented as a registration. And it contradicts E-PRED-B, which the predictions page marks LOCKED.

anticipated_objections.objection: Low Sun at EBR/NGK/BDV makes geometric obscuration misleading.
anticipated_objections.response: Disclosed in the source line. Sun altitude at max: EBR 4.8, NGK 3.5, BDV 1.0 deg. All are above the horizon, so the maximum obscuration is still visible. For the magnetic effect the relevant shadow is on the E-region (~110 km), which is sunlit at all of them.

anticipated_objections.objection: We used the dome's 2-dp coordinates, not IAGA coordinates.
anticipated_objections.response: Deliberate: the comparison is with the dome's table. Differences from rev4 (IAGA header coordinates) are <=0.0001.

sensitivities_and_limits: Obscuration computed with DE421 (not DE440s, which 4.2.7 cites for Hartland). Agreement at Hartland 0.9436 vs 4.2.7 94% (magnitude 0.949 both). Not a material difference for pp-level comparisons.
An independent NASA local-circumstances cross-check is still recommended (same open recommendation as rev4 methods.obscuration).
